title: The new checkout UI converts better overall — make it the default?

scenario.role: You're the checkout-experience analyst at Coastline Goods
scenario.situation: A contextual policy rolled the new checkout UI out more aggressively on mobile first, before ramping desktop. Looking at overall conversion across all traffic, Priya, the head of Product, sees the new UI converting higher than the old one and wants to make it the permanent default for all devices.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Across all traffic, the new checkout UI converts better than the old one. Let's make it the default everywhere."
scenario.question: Did the new UI actually convert better within mobile and within desktop, or does the overall number just reflect how traffic was allocated? Split the comparison by device before making it the default.

columns.name: arm
columns.description: new_ui or old_ui — which checkout UI this session was shown (allocated unevenly by device — mobile got new_ui far more often than desktop did)

columns.name: converted
columns.description: 1 if the session completed checkout — the reward

guidingQuestions: Reproduce Priya's number: mean converted for arm == new_ui versus old_ui, pooled across all sessions. How big is the win?
What share of sessions got new_ui on mobile versus on desktop? Was the new UI allocated evenly across devices?
Now compute the new_ui vs. old_ui conversion gap SEPARATELY within mobile and within desktop. Does the new UI actually win in either segment?
Compare mobile's overall conversion rate to desktop's, regardless of UI. Which device converts higher, and how does that interact with which UI got more traffic on which device?
If the new UI loses within every device segment but wins pooled, what is the pooled number actually measuring?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the pooled gap: mean(converted) for new_ui minus old_ui across all sessions.
Check the share of new_ui within mobile sessions and within desktop sessions separately — look for an uneven allocation.
Split the conversion comparison by device: compute the new_ui vs. old_ui gap within mobile only, then within desktop only.
Compare baseline conversion rates by device to see whether one device converts substantially higher than the other regardless of UI.
Explain how an uneven traffic split across a higher- and lower-converting segment can flip the pooled sign relative to every individual segment — classic Simpson's paradox.

notebook.intro: Five steps: reproduce the pooled win, check how the traffic was split, then compare the arms on equal ground.

cells.title: Reproduce the pooled gap
cells.explain: Start with the exact claim on the table — new_ui's conversion minus old_ui's, across every session.
cells.code:
rates = df.groupby("arm")["converted"].mean() * 100
pooled_gap = rates["new_ui"] - rates["old_ui"]
print(f"pooled gap (new_ui - old_ui): {pooled_gap:+.2f} pts")
rates.round(2)
cells.reads: The pooled number really does favour new_ui. Everything that follows is about whether the comparison behind it is fair.

cells.title: Check how the traffic was split
cells.explain: A bandit allocates traffic; it does not run a coin flip. Look at what share of each device's sessions went to each arm.
cells.code:
mix = pd.crosstab(df["device"], df["arm"], normalize="index") * 100
print("share of each arm within each device (%)")
mix.round(1)
cells.reads: The split leans opposite ways on the two devices. That alone makes the pooled comparison a comparison of device mixes, not of interfaces.

cells.title: Compare the arms within each device
cells.explain: Hold the device constant and the allocation stops mattering. This is the like-for-like comparison.
cells.code:
by_device = df.groupby(["device", "arm"])["converted"].mean().unstack() * 100
by_device["gap"] = by_device["new_ui"] - by_device["old_ui"]
by_device.round(2)
cells.reads: Look at the sign of the gap column on both rows, then compare it with the pooled gap from cell 1.

cells.title: See which device converts better anyway
cells.explain: For a mix to flip a result, the segments have to differ in the outcome as well as in allocation. Check that here.
cells.code:
baseline = df.groupby("device")["converted"].mean() * 100
print("conversion by device, ignoring the arm (%)")
baseline.round(2)
cells.reads: One device converts far better regardless of interface — and it is the device new_ui was given most of.

cells.title: Put the two numbers side by side
cells.explain: Re-weight both arms to one common device mix, so neither is flattered by where its traffic came from.
cells.code:
within = df.groupby(["device", "arm"])["converted"].mean().unstack()
weights = df["device"].value_counts(normalize=True)
adjusted = within.mul(weights, axis=0).sum() * 100
adj_gap = adjusted["new_ui"] - adjusted["old_ui"]
print(f"mix-adjusted gap: {adj_gap:+.2f} pts")
pd.DataFrame({"effect (pts)": [pooled_gap, adj_gap]}, index=["pooled", "mix-adjusted"]).round(2)
cells.reads: The sign flips once both arms face the same device mix. The pooled number was measuring the allocation, not the interface.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Pooled across all sessions, the new checkout UI converts better than the old one. That reads as a clear win — obviously make it the default everywhere.
teachingNote.theTrap: The rollout policy didn't allocate the new UI evenly: mobile sessions got new_ui 76% of the time, while desktop sessions got it only 25% of the time (a mobile-first ramp). Mobile also converts substantially higher than desktop regardless of which UI is shown. Split the comparison by device and the new UI actually LOSES in both: -0.7 points on mobile and -1.9 points on desktop. But because the new UI's traffic is disproportionately mobile (the higher-converting segment) and the old UI's traffic is disproportionately desktop (the lower-converting segment), the pooled comparison mixes a favorable segment for the new UI with an unfavorable one for the old UI — and the pooled number flips positive even though the new UI never actually wins anywhere. This is Simpson's paradox, driven here by unequal bandit/rollout traffic allocation rather than a random split.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Always split a bandit or rollout comparison by the segments traffic was allocated across, especially when the allocation itself wasn't uniform. Here, the honest, segment-level answer is that the old UI converts better on both mobile (-0.7 points for new_ui) and desktop (-1.9 points for new_ui) — the pooled +1.1 point 'win' is entirely a traffic-mix artifact of the mobile-first rollout, not a real effect of the new UI. Tell Priya: don't make the new UI the default. If anything, the data argues for keeping the old UI, or investigating why the new UI underperforms on both platforms before shipping it anywhere.
howToGetThere: Compute the pooled gap: mean(converted | new_ui) minus mean(converted | old_ui) across all sessions ≈ +1.1 points.
Check new_ui's share by device: 76% on mobile vs. 25% on desktop — a strongly uneven allocation from the rollout policy.
Split the gap by device: mobile ≈ -0.7 points (old_ui wins), desktop ≈ -1.9 points (old_ui wins) — new_ui loses in both segments.
Compare device baseline conversion: mobile converts meaningfully higher than desktop regardless of UI — the segment new_ui got more of is simply an easier-converting segment.
Conclude: the pooled 'win' is a mix-shift artifact of unequal traffic allocation, not a real effect of the new UI — Simpson's paradox.

numbers.label: new_ui share of traffic: mobile vs. desktop

teachingNote.lesson: A bandit or phased rollout that allocates traffic unevenly across segments — even for good operational reasons, like ramping mobile first — can produce a pooled result that reverses what's true in every individual segment, the same Simpson's paradox mechanism as any confounded observational comparison. Whenever an arm's traffic share differs across a variable that also affects the outcome, split the comparison by that variable before trusting the pooled number. A policy that loses in every segment cannot be a real winner overall — the pooled 'win' is measuring the traffic mix, not the policy.
